Revised manuscript accepted 23 August 2001. The Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Late Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the Fennoscandian Shield. The TIB was formed at c. 1.85–1.67 Ga (Ahl et al. 1999) along the southwestern boundary of the Svecofennian Domain (Gaál & Gorbatschev 1987). It defines a belt of igneous rocks that ex- tends

e-mar- gin process (e.g. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova 1993), and plate tectonic models proposed that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed by compression (Windley 1993). However, Ahl et al. (1999) present a model suggesting that the Dala granit- oids in the central part of the TIB were formed in a period of tran- sition between subduction-related compression (1.81–1.77 Ga) and an extensive environment (1.70–1.68 Ga). The Rätan granite (e.g. Lundegårdh 1967; Lundqvist 1968), which forms a large intrusion north and east of the Dala granitoids, was emplaced at c. 1.70 Ga (U–Pb, Wilson et al. 1985; Patchett et al. 1987; Delin 1996). Sparse AMS data from the granite indicate that it may have formed in an extensive tectonic regime (Mattsson & Elming 2001). In this study new AMS data from the Rätan granite are pre- sented in order to better constrain the results from Mattsson & Elming (2001) and to test whether or not the granite was em- placed in an extensive tectonic regime. We also discuss new paleomagnetic results from the Rätan granitoid batholith. GFF , Vol. 123 (Pt. 4, December), pp. 205–215. Stockholm. ISSN 1103-5897. Abstract: The 1.85–1.67 Ga Transscandinavian Igneous Belt (TIB) forms a major Paleoproterozoic igneous complex in the western part of the Fennoscandian Shield. Different tectonic models propose that the TIB was formed in a tectonic regime governed either by compression or by extension. This paper presents an analysis of anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) and paleomagnetic data from the Rätan granite (1.70 Ga), which forms a large pluton in the central part of the TIB. The major aim of the study is to test the existing tectonic models and to de- fine a paleomagnetic pole position for the Rätan granite. Three contrast- ing magnetic fabric domains are identified. In the eastern and western domains the AMS fabric is characterized by NW–SE to N–S trending subvertical foliation planes and a girdle distribution of the maximum and intermediate anisotropy axes. The central domain is characterized by subhorizontal magnetic foliation planes and lineations that cluster in a NW–SE trending direction. We suggest that the Rätan granite was emplaced in

Conclusion of rock magnetic experiments The remanent magnetization of the Morelos lime- stone was carried by goethite and magnetite in variable proportions, with minor hematite. The Tecomazuchil and Rosario sandstones contained the same minerals, but hematite in the form of pigment and specularite was present in larger concentrations in many samples. paleomagnetic studies: the Rosario Formation, the lower part of the Jurassic Tecomazuchil, and the Cretaceous Morelos Formation. Locations of the sampling sites are indi- cated in Fig. 1. The Tecomazuchil Formation was sampled in stratigraphic order over a total height of 13 m in 11 beds, and magnetostratigraphic results have already been published (Urrutia-Fucugauchi et al., 1990). The Morelos Formation was sampled in 8 beds covering a total thickness of 18 m. Roughly 50 km further to the south, the Rosario Formation was sampled in 12 beds with a total thickness of 7 m. Here the overlaying Tecocoyunca Group has been studied as well, but the paleomagnetic results showed strong, unremovable secondary overprints and were therefore of no tectonic relevance (Bo ¨hnel, 1985). The rocks were sampled using a portable gasoline- powered drill with diamond drill bits, and the cores were oriented in situ with an inclinometer and a mag- netic compass (Collinson, 1983). Sampling was done in stratigraphic order, taking 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. In this manner 31 cores from the Morelos lime- stone were obtained, 38 cores from the Tecomazuchil sandstone, and 35 cores from the Rosario Formation. king 3–4 cores per horizon to check for the internal consistency of the magnetic record. In this manner 31 cores from the Morelos lime- stone were obtained, 38 cores from the Tecomazuchil sandstone, and 35 cores from the Rosario Formation. For laboratory studies cores were later cut into 21 mm long specimens. Di erent magnetometers were used to determine the intensity and direction of the natural remanent magne- tization (NRM): a Digico ﬂuxgate spinner magnet- ometer was used for some of the specimens but, due to the rather low NRM-intensites, a SQUID magnet- ometer was also used. Conclusion of rock magnetic experiments The remanent magnetization of the Morelos lime- stone was carried by goethite and magnetite in variable proportions, with minor hematite. The Tecomazuchil and Rosario sandstones contained the same minerals, but hematite in the form of pigment and specularite was present in larger concentrations in many samples. Conclusion of rock magnetic experiments The remanent magnetization of the Morelos lime- stone was carried by goethite and magnetite in variable proportions, with minor hematite. Since there is no younger early Paleozoic paleomagnetic pole yet available for the Argentine Precordillera, its kinematic history between the Early Cambrian and the Late Ordovician remains unconstrained by paleo- magnetic data. rio de Paleomagnetismo Daniel Valencio, Departamento de Ciencias Geológicas, FCEyN, Universidad de Buenos Aires, Pabellón 2, Ciudad Universidaria, 1428 Buenos Aires, Argentina ABSTRACT The Paleozoic evolution of southwestern Gondwana apparently involved the accre- tion of several large suspect terranes at different times and under different tectonic circumstances. The recent acquisition of paleomagnetic data from Paleozoic rocks of this region, albeit still scarce, permit establishment of some constrains on the tectonic and paleogeographic evolution of some of these terranes. A reliable paleomagnetic pole from the Early Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation in northern Precordillera confirms that the Argentine Precordillera is an exotic terrane that was part of or adjacent to Laurentia, very likely at the Ouachita Embayment, in the Early Cambrian. Paleomag- netic poles from an Early Ordovician magmatic belt in northwest Argentina permit the identification of a peri-Gondwanic–rotated terrane, called the Eastern Puna–Famatina terrane, with volcanic arc affinities. Early Paleozoic paleomagnetic poles from the Western Puna (Sierra de Almeida, Chile) were previously interpreted as evidence of a para-autochthonous nature of the Arequipa-Antofalla Massif that rotated successively clockwise and counter

Despite this being known for several decades (Poulsen, 1958; Borrello, 1965), it was not until much later (Ramos et al., 1986; Dalla Salda et al., 1992; Astini et al., 1995) that the possi- bility of the Argentine Precordillera being an accreted terrane was considered seriously. Until very recently, no paleomagnetic data were available to test and constrain the tectonic models mentioned before. This was due, in part to the few paleomagnetic studies carried out on this region, but also to an apparently widespread and pervasive Permian remagnetizing event that inhibited determination of the primary magnetic components from many of the Lower Paleozoic rocks (Rapalini and Tarling, 1993; Truco and Rapalini, 1996). A successful paleomagnetic study was recently carried out on the Lower Cambrian Cerro Totora Formation (Rapalini and Astini, 1998), exposed in the northern Precordillera (location 1 in Fig. 1). The Cerro Totora Formation consists in a mixed suc- cession of evaporites, red siliciclastics, and carbonates (Astini and Vaccari, 1996) with trilobites of the Bonnia-Olenellus zone (Vaccari, 1990). This succession has been interpreted as typical synrift deposits (Astini and Vaccari, 1996), possibly accumulated during the initial rifting of the Argentine Precordillera from the Ouachita embayment of south-central North America (Thomas and Astini, 1996). The susceptibility of multi-domain (MD) grains is con- trolled mainly by magnetocrystalline anisotropy (Uyeda et al., 1963) which is strongly temperature dependent: magnetite undergoes a structural change known as the Verwey transition at ÿ1508C. Medium to high grade polymetamorphic terranes occur along the northern margin of the Huabei (North China) Shield as inliers exposed beneath supracrustal successions comprising the Meso-Neoproterozoic Jixian Supergroup. Cooling of these terranes and their elevation to present surface levels occurred prior to de- position of the oldest part of the Jixian succession at 01850 Ma. s is a bulk parameter recording preferred mineral orientation by metamorphic crystallisation and/or ﬂow mechan- isms. The grains contributing to this e ect have para- magnetic and ferromagnetic properties; the paramagnetic minerals are mostly the iron-bearing sili- cates whilst the ferromagnetic contribution is from magnetite, and sometimes pyrrhotite or hematite. The strong ferromagnetic e ect of the small volume of these latter grains is often much larger than the para- magnetic and (weak negative) diamagnetic e ects of the bulk silicate matrix. Whilst the inﬂuence of fabric on the dilute amounts of ferromagnetic grains in which the stable remanence resides cannot be isolated by study of AMS, it is a useful qualitative indicator of bias of magnetic remanence by fabric; a comparison between results from samples of strong and weak fab- rics at the same site is often able to recognise the likely importance of any such bias. Medium to high grade polymetamorphic terranes occur along the northern margin of the Huabei (North China) Shield as inliers exposed beneath supracrustal successions comprising the Meso-Neoproterozoic Jixian Supergroup. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. he ﬁnal phase of subduction-related magmatism at this margin of Avalonia. Following cessation of volcanism, a transgressing sea deposited limestones, shales, mudstones and greywackes between Late Caradoc and Ludlow times. This succession forms the Winderemere Supergroup and makes up the Silurian outcrop in Figure 1. During burial and subsequent Acadian deformation the Lower Palaeozoic rocks of the Lake District were metamorphosed to no higher than lower greenschist grade, in common with the paratectonic Caledonides of Wales; this was insucient to comprehensively remagnetize pre-Acadian rocks which are reported widely to retain an Ordovician remanence record (Briden and Morris, 1973; Piper et al., 1978; Piper, 1979; Channell and McCabe, 1992). In addition to the basic plutonism noted above, acidic magmatism occurred at various stages between the intense mid-Ordovician volcanic events and the culmination of tectonic activity in the Acadian episode. A general distinction is recognized between earlier Na-rich activity and later more K-rich activity (Piper et al., 1978). The Carrock Fell and Ennerdale Granophyres are typical sub-volcanic plutons, whilst the Threlkeld– St John’sbody is a microgranite with small phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene suggesting near-liquidus compositions (O’Br

ents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times. Strategy of investigation and previous studies The granitic batholith represents an extensive late-Caledonian thermal inﬂuence with e ectswidely recorded by metasomatism in the acid plutons and by hydrothermal mineral veins in the country rocks (O’Brien et al., 1985). Hence palaeomagnetic analysis needs to address the extent of magnetic overprinting by this event. Unfortunately the granites are mostly composed of coarse leucocratic quartz–feldspar assemblages unsuitable for palaeomagnetic study. Accordingly they are investigated here (Skiddaw, Shap and Eskdale Granites) largely in terms of thermal overprinting of adjoining country rocks; in addition the Shap Granite is reddened and partially retains a stable ancient remanence whilst the Ennerdale Granophyre is intruded by basic bodies probably only a little younger than the age of granophyre emplacement. Collective investigation of these plutons allows the partial overprinting e ectsof the Late Caledonian thermal event to be recognized in the older Ordovician igneous bodies. With the exception of gentle folding linked to the Variscan Episode and post-Variscan rifting, the region has been quiescent since Caledonian times, although uplifted with removal of 2–3 km of overburden since early Tertiary times.
